questions.question: What is the consensus problem in distributed systems?
options: Deciding which programming language to use for a distributed application
Getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value or sequence of operations despite failures
Determining the optimal number of servers in a cluster
Choosing the fastest network protocol for inter-node communication
questions.explanation: Consensus is the problem of getting multiple distributed nodes to agree on the same value or the same order of operations, even when some nodes may crash or messages may be delayed. It's fundamental to replicated state machines, leader election, and distributed transactions.

questions.question: In Raft, what are the three possible states of a node?
options: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary
Leader, Follower, Candidate
Master, Slave, Observer
Active, Standby, Failed
questions.explanation: In Raft, every node is in one of three states: Leader (handles all client requests and replicates logs), Follower (passively receives log entries from the leader), or Candidate (temporarily, during an election when the leader is suspected to have failed).

questions.question: What triggers a leader election in Raft?
options: A new node joins the cluster
A follower's election timeout expires without receiving a heartbeat from the leader
The cluster reaches maximum capacity
An administrator manually initiates the election
questions.explanation: Each follower has a randomized election timeout. If a follower doesn't receive a heartbeat from the leader before this timeout expires, it assumes the leader has failed, transitions to Candidate state, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from other nodes.

questions.question: What does the FLP impossibility result state?
options: It is impossible to build a reliable network
In a purely asynchronous system where even one node can crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus
Distributed databases cannot scale beyond 100 nodes
Paxos and Raft are fundamentally flawed algorithms
questions.explanation: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result proves that in a fully asynchronous distributed system (no timing assumptions), there is no deterministic consensus algorithm that is guaranteed to terminate if even one node can fail. Practical systems work around this using timeouts, randomization, and partial synchrony assumptions.

questions.question: Why does Raft require a majority (quorum) of nodes to agree before committing a log entry?
options: To ensure all nodes have identical data at all times
To guarantee that any two quorums overlap by at least one node, preventing conflicting decisions
To reduce network traffic by involving fewer nodes
Because minority nodes are always offline
questions.explanation: Any two majorities of an N-node cluster must share at least one node. This overlap ensures that a newly elected leader will always find at least one node that knows about the latest committed entry. Without majority quorum, two partitions could independently commit conflicting values.

questions.question: What are the two phases of the basic Paxos protocol?
options: Lock and Unlock
Prepare (Promise) and Accept (Commit)
Read and Write
Propose and Reject
questions.explanation: In Paxos, the Prepare phase has the proposer sending a proposal number to acceptors, who promise not to accept lower-numbered proposals. In the Accept phase, if the proposer gets promises from a majority, it sends the actual value to be accepted. This two-phase approach ensures safety even with concurrent proposers.

questions.question: What role do ZooKeeper and etcd play in distributed architectures?
options: They serve as high-throughput message queues
They provide consensus-based coordination services for leader election, configuration management, and distributed locks
They are load balancers that distribute HTTP traffic
They are monitoring tools that track server health
questions.explanation: ZooKeeper and etcd are distributed coordination services built on consensus algorithms (ZAB for ZooKeeper, Raft for etcd). They provide primitives like distributed locks, leader election, service discovery, and configuration storage. Kubernetes uses etcd as its sole source of truth for cluster state.

questions.question: A Raft cluster has 5 nodes. The leader sends a log entry to all followers. Nodes 1 (leader), 2, and 3 acknowledge the entry, but nodes 4 and 5 are slow and haven't responded. Can the leader commit the entry?
options: No, it must wait for all 5 nodes to respond
Yes, 3 out of 5 nodes (including the leader) form a majority, so the entry can be committed
No, it needs at least 4 nodes to agree
Yes, but only if nodes 4 and 5 are confirmed crashed
questions.explanation: Raft requires a majority quorum to commit. With 5 nodes, the majority is 3. Since the leader (node 1) plus nodes 2 and 3 have the entry — that's 3 nodes — the leader can safely commit. Nodes 4 and 5 will receive the entry eventually and catch up. The system continues operating despite their slowness.

questions.question: In a 5-node Raft cluster, the leader (Node A) becomes network-partitioned from Nodes D and E but can still reach B and C. Nodes D and E elect a new leader among themselves. What prevents this split-brain scenario from causing data inconsistency?
options: Both leaders operate independently and merge data later
D and E cannot elect a leader because they form only 2 out of 5 nodes — below the majority quorum of 3
The old leader automatically steps down when it detects any network issue
A central arbiter service resolves the conflict
questions.explanation: In a 5-node cluster, a candidate needs 3 votes to win an election. Nodes D and E are only 2 nodes — they cannot form a majority. Meanwhile, Node A with B and C forms a group of 3 and can continue operating as leader with quorum. The majority quorum requirement inherently prevents split-brain scenarios.

questions.question: Why did the designers of Raft explicitly prioritize understandability over Paxos, and what structural decision makes Raft easier to implement correctly?
options: Raft uses a simpler hash function than Paxos
Raft decomposes consensus into independent subproblems (leader election, log replication, safety) and uses a strong leader model, whereas Paxos treats consensus more monolithically
Raft requires fewer nodes than Paxos
Raft avoids using network communication entirely
questions.explanation: Raft's designers (Ongaro and Ousterhout) found that Paxos was notoriously difficult to understand and implement correctly. Raft uses a strong single-leader model and cleanly separates the consensus problem into leader election, log replication, and safety — each independently understandable. This decomposition reduces implementation bugs and has made Raft the preferred consensus algorithm in modern systems like etcd and CockroachDB.
